definition: In philosophy of logic, defeasible reasoning is a kind of provisional reasoning that is rationally compelling, though not deductively valid.
details: It usually occurs when a rule is given, but there may be specific exceptions to the rule, or subclasses that are subject to a different rule. Defeasibility is found in literatures that are concerned with argument and the process of argument, or heuristic reasoning. Defeasible reasoning is a particular kind of non-demonstrative reasoning, where the reasoning does not produce a full, complete, or final demonstration of a claim, i.e., where fallibility and corrigibility of a conclusion are acknowledged. In other words, defeasible reasoning produces a contingent statement or claim. Defeasible reasoning is also a kind of ampliative reasoning because its conclusions reach beyond the pure meanings of the premises. Defeasible reasoning finds its fullest expression in jurisprudence, ethics and moral philosophy, epistemology, pragmatics and conversational conventions in linguistics, constructivist decision theories, and in knowledge representation and planning in artificial intelligence. It is also closely identified with prima facie (presumptive) reasoning (i.e., reasoning on the "face" of evidence), and ceteris paribus (default) reasoning (i.e., reasoning, all things "being equal"). explainer.lead: Defeasible reasoning means drawing a reasonable conclusion while accepting that new information could overturn it. It helps people and AI systems act under general rules that have exceptions, without pretending their conclusions are guaranteed.

tiers.eli5: If the sidewalk is wet, you might reasonably decide that it rained. If someone then tells you a sprinkler was running, you change your mind even though the sidewalk is still wet. This is reasoning with the best answer you have for now, while staying ready to correct it.
tiers.practitioner: In knowledge representation and planning, defeasible reasoning supports default rules, specific exceptions, and conclusions that must be revised as facts arrive. A practical design should distinguish a provisional conclusion from a deductively valid one and record what would defeat it. Pitfalls include treating defaults as universal rules, overlooking exceptional subclasses, and leaving outdated conclusions in place after an exception appears.
tiers.paperLevel: A conclusion C is defeasible when premises P rationally support C but do not deductively entail it, so additional information E can defeat C without falsifying P. The conclusion is contingent and corrigible, and it may be ampliative: its content goes beyond the pure meanings of the premises. It is closely associated with prima facie reasoning from presumptive evidence and ceteris paribus reasoning under an all-things-equal assumption.

explainer.example: Suppose the rule is that birds can fly, and Tweety is a bird, so you provisionally conclude that Tweety can fly. Learning that Tweety is a penguin introduces an exception, so you withdraw that conclusion while keeping both original premises: Tweety is still a bird, and the general rule was never a guarantee for every bird.

usedIn.name: Jurisprudence
usedIn.detail: Legal conclusions can be supported by general rules while remaining open to exceptions and further argument.

usedIn.name: Ethics and moral philosophy
usedIn.detail: Moral judgments may rely on presumptions that can be defeated by relevant circumstances.

usedIn.name: AI knowledge representation and planning
usedIn.detail: Systems can use general rules with exceptions and revise provisional conclusions when new facts arrive.

usedIn.name: Linguistic pragmatics
usedIn.detail: Conversational interpretations can be reasonable on the available evidence yet open to correction.

explainer.intuition: A conclusion can be rationally compelling without being guaranteed. Defeasible reasoning makes that provisional status explicit, so new evidence can defeat the conclusion without making the original premises false.
howItWorks: Start with the available facts and a general rule.
Apply the rule to reach a provisional conclusion.
Acknowledge that the conclusion is not deductively guaranteed.
Check for exceptions, special subclasses, or other defeating information.
Keep, revise, or withdraw the conclusion as the information changes.
explainer.whyItMatters: Many rules are useful without being exceptionless, and many decisions must be made before every relevant fact is known. Defeasible reasoning supports justified action while preserving the ability to correct conclusions.
misconceptions: It is not merely careless or fallacious reasoning.
A defeated conclusion does not mean the original premises were false.
It is not deductively valid reasoning with a weaker name.
